transfer_rules.rule_summary: Singapore lifted its exchange controls in 1978. You do not need any exchange-control approval to send money out of or bring money into Singapore, though normal bank anti-money-laundering checks still apply.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: no exchange control formalities or approvals are required for all forms of payments or capital transfers

transfer_rules.rule_name: Bank wire transfers up to S$1,500: sender and recipient details
transfer_rules.rule_summary: For any cross-border wire transfer of S$1,500 or less, the sending bank must include your name and account number plus the recipient's name and account number. Have the recipient's exact name and account details ready.
documents_required: Originator account number or unique transaction reference
Beneficiary account number or unique transaction reference
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: In a cross-border wire transfer where the amount to be transferred is below or equal to S$1,500

transfer_rules.rule_name: Bank wire transfers above S$1,500: extra sender identifier
transfer_rules.rule_summary: For a cross-border wire transfer above S$1,500, the bank must also send one extra piece of information about you: your address, your ID number, or your date and place of birth.
documents_required: One of: originator address, originator unique identification number, or originator date and place of birth
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: In a cross-border wire transfer where the amount to be transferred exceeds S$1,500

transfer_rules.rule_name: Receiving bank checks incoming wire transfers
transfer_rules.rule_summary: When money arrives from overseas, your Singapore bank must verify your identity if it has not already done so. It can hold, reject or follow up on transfers that are missing sender or recipient details, so ask senders to give your exact name and account number.
documents_required: Beneficiary identity verification (if not previously verified)
transfer_rules.restrictions: Transfers lacking required originator or beneficiary information may be executed, rejected or suspended under the bank's risk-based policies.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: shall identify and verify the identity of the wire transfer beneficiary

transfer_rules.rule_name: Remittance companies: same S$1,500 information rule
transfer_rules.rule_summary: Licensed payment and remittance companies follow the same rule as banks. Above S$1,500 they must verify who you are and send your address, ID number or date and place of birth along with the transfer.
documents_required: Originator name and account number or reference
Beneficiary name and account number or reference
Above S$1,500: originator residential address, unique identification number, or date and place of birth
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: the wire transfer originator's unique identification number

transfer_rules.rule_name: ID check for one-off cross-border remittances
transfer_rules.rule_summary: If you use a remittance company without an existing account relationship, it must check your identity (customer due diligence) for any cross-border transfer, whatever the amount. Bring your passport or pass.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Applies to customers without an existing business relationship with the payment service provider.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: any funds by cross-border wire transfer

transfer_rules.rule_name: Declare cash over S$20,000 at the border
transfer_rules.rule_summary: If you carry, post or ship cash or bearer instruments (e.g. traveller's cheques) worth more than S$20,000 (or the foreign-currency equivalent) into or out of Singapore, you must file a report. Travellers can do this online via ICA or the MyICA app.
documents_required: Form NP 727 (traveller) or Form NP 728 (sender, carrier or recipient by cargo/post)
transfer_rules.restrictions: Failure to report: fine not exceeding S$50,000, imprisonment not exceeding 3 years, or both; cash may be seized.
transfer_rules.regulator: Singapore Police Force (Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office)
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: exceeding SGD 20,000 (the prescribed amount) or its equivalent in a foreign currency into or out of Singapore

transfer_rules.rule_name: Foreign-sourced income received by resident individuals is tax-exempt
transfer_rules.rule_summary: Since 1 January 2004, foreign-sourced income received in Singapore by tax-resident individuals is exempt from Singapore income tax, unless it is received through a partnership in Singapore.
transfer_rules.restrictions: Stated for resident individuals; income received through a partnership in Singapore is excluded.
transfer_rules.exceptions: Income received through a partnership in Singapore.
transfer_rules.evidence_quote: From 1 Jan 2004, all foreign-sourced income received by resident individuals not through a partnership in Singapore

account_opening.summary: Foreign students holding a Student's Pass can open a savings account with the major Singapore banks. Banks typically ask for a valid passport, the Student's Pass (or a school letter), and proof of a residential address in Singapore. Some banks let foreigners apply in-app (DBS digibank, HSBC app via Myinfo or document upload). UOB says new foreign customers must visit a branch with original documents, and OCBC requires foreign students to submit their school letter at a branch. Minimum ages and pass requirements differ by bank and account.
typical_documents: Valid passport (DBS: must not be expired; OCBC and UOB: at least 6 months validity)
Student's Pass, or an official certification letter from the educational institution (DBS: dated within 3 months)
Proof of residential address: e.g. school certification letter (DBS), faculty/hall residence letter (OCBC), utility/telco bill, bank statement, tenancy agreement or government letter (SC)
Proof of tax residency, e.g. passport or national identity card (DBS)
eligibility_factors: Holding a valid pass (DBS lists Employment Pass, S Pass, Student Pass, or In-Principle Approval from MOM or ICA)
Minimum age differs by account (OCBC FRANK: 16; SC JumpStart: 18 to 26; HSBC online application: 18; DBS My Account: no age restriction stated)
Living in Singapore with a valid local residential address (P.O. Box, care-of, office and school addresses not accepted by DBS)
Name and FIN on documents must match the application (DBS)
Channel: UOB says new foreign customers must visit a branch with original documents; photocopies or digital copies not accepted

banks.visa_requirements: Valid pass such as Employment Pass, S Pass, Student Pass, or In-Principle Approval from MOM or ICA
documents: Student pass or certification letter from school (dated within 3 months; name and FIN must match application)
Proof of residential address, e.g. certification letter from school (P.O. Box, care-of, office and school addresses not acceptable)
Proof of tax residency, e.g. passport or national identity card
banks.minimum_balance: No minimum balance and no initial deposit required
banks.monthly_fee: S$2 per month if not enrolled in e-statements; waived for customers up to 16 years old or enrolled in e-statements
banks.credit_card_available: Foreigners: minimum gross annual income S$45K and an eligible work pass such as Employment Pass or S Pass; principal cardholders 21 to 75 years old. No student provision stated.
banks.evidence_quote: You'll need a valid pass such as a Student Pass or other approved passes from MOM or ICA.
banks.notes: My Account page states 'No age restriction' for minimum age. DBS Remit: 'Send money to 50+ destinations with same day transfers and no fees.' No dedicated student account found on the pages fetched. Sources also: https://www.dbs.com.sg/personal/deposits/savings-accounts/my-account, https://www.dbs.com.sg/personal/support/bank-account-opening-documents-required.html, https://www.dbs.com.sg/personal/support/card-application-eligibility.html

banks.account_type: OCBC FRANK Account (savings with FRANK debit card)
banks.visa_requirements: Foreigners need a valid pass, e.g. Employment Pass, S-Pass or Student Pass
documents: Passport with validity of at least 6 months
Proof of address dated within last 3 months (phone bill, CPF statement, bank statement, or government letter)
Foreign students: original faculty/hall residence letter from school, submitted at an OCBC branch
banks.minimum_balance: Initial deposit S$0; no minimum average balance stated
banks.credit_card_available: OCBC FRANK Credit Card: principal cardholders 21 years old; foreigners at least S$45,000 annual income. No student provision stated.
banks.evidence_quote: Singaporean, Singapore PR or foreigner with a valid pass.
banks.notes: Overseas transfers via OCBC Online Banking in 19 currencies; minimum SGD 100 or USD 100 per transaction; payee full name, address, account number/IBAN and SWIFT code required (https://www.ocbc.com/personal-banking/digital-banking/overseas-funds-transfer.page). FRANK Debit Card foreign transactions: 3.25% fee and 2.80% currency conversion fee. Credit card source: https://www.ocbc.com/personal-banking/cards/ocbc-frank-credit-card

banks.visa_requirements: UOB accounts FAQ lists Employment Pass/S Pass/Dependent Pass for new foreign customers; Student Pass not listed there
documents: Proof of residential address (e.g. latest utilities or telecom bills)
Pass (FAQ lists Employment Pass/S Pass/Dependent Pass)
Originals only; photocopied or digital copies not accepted; branch visit required for new foreign customers
banks.minimum_balance: No minimum deposit for Uniplus; no minimum balance on selected UOB accounts (tertiary students page)
banks.monthly_fee: No fall-below fees on selected UOB accounts; 3-year fee waiver on selected accounts and debit cards for applicants aged 16 to 24
banks.credit_card_available: UOB EVOL Card: 21 years and above; foreigners S$40,000 p.a. No student credit card mentioned on the tertiary students page.
banks.evidence_quote: International students needing simple, low-maintenance banking
banks.notes: Conflict: UOB's foreigner guide recommends Uniplus for international students, but its accounts FAQ (https://www.uob.com.sg/personal/customer-service/accounts.page) lists only Employment Pass/S Pass/Dependent Pass. Overseas transfer page found only covers TMRW transfers to Malaysia (DuitNow) and Thailand (PromptPay) by phone number. Uniplus product page did not show eligibility/fees in fetched text. Other sources: https://www.uob.com.sg/personal/highlights/life-moments/adulting/tertiary-students.page, https://www.uob.com.sg/personal/cards/cashback/evol-card/index.page

documents: Proof of address, any of: last 3 months' utility bill, last 3 months' bank statement, telecommunications bill, tenancy agreement, or government-issued document stating address (e.g. IRAS, CPF, ICA)
banks.monthly_fee: No fall-below fee and no monthly fee

SC Remit: 'Send money to more than 50 markets' (https://www.sc.com/sg/bank-with-us/remittance/). Credit card source: https://www.sc.com/sg/credit-cards/smart-credit-card/ (income criteria shown as a single set; re-check for foreigner-specific rules).

banks.evidence_quote: If you hold a valid FIN and reside in Singapore, you'll need to upload your passport copy and proof of address.
banks.notes: The age of 18 applies to online applications. Residents of US, Canada, France or Jersey cannot apply via the app. Global Money Transfers: 'Send money internationally faster and fee-free to over 50 countries/territories.' Minimum balance and fall-below fee could not be confirmed (the tariff PDF table was garbled). what_contributes: Credit payment history collected across banks and major financial institutions
Loans and credit card applications, and repayment records
Score factors: utilisation pattern, available credit, late payments on loan accounts, credit account history, enquiry activity, recent credit
why_it_matters: Banks and other financial institutions assess your creditworthiness by looking at your score and other factors such as income
A good credit repayment history makes it easier to qualify for loans and credit cards in the future
More loan applications are linked to higher credit risk
responsible_behaviours: Pay your bills in full and on time, and stay within your spending limits
Avoid taking multiple loans in a short time
Pay down debts as much as possible
Check your credit report regularly to catch issues early
If you find an error, dispute it; the licensed bureau or your financial institution will investigate, and corrected records are sent to members who accessed the report in the last 12 months
risks: Every default or late payment could affect your score
Many credit applications in a short period can count against you
